column1: According to Kenneth Arrow (1963), what is the defining characteristic that separates healthcare from ordinary commodities?
column2: Information asymmetry/uncertainty: patients cannot observe physician effort, diagnostic accuracy, or treatment necessity, unlike quality-observable ordinary goods.

column1: What is the principal-agent problem in healthcare provision, and why does it create a conflict of interest?
column2: Physicians (agents) make consumption decisions on behalf of patients (principals) who lack technical knowledge to evaluate recommendations; since physicians also profit from treatment volume, they face incentives to over-recommend services.

column1: What is Supplier-Induced Demand (SID), and what empirical pattern supports it?
column2: SID is when providers exploit informational advantage to shift patient utilization beyond the welfare-maximizing level. Empirically, regions with higher physician density show higher utilization rates even after controlling for population health status.

column1: In McGuire's physician agency model, what two arguments does the physician's utility function U(I, θ) depend on?
column2: Income (I), derived from volume/intensity of services (I = Σ pᵢqᵢ), and a professional ethical norm parameter (θ) that penalizes deviation from clinically appropriate care.

column1: What distinguishes adverse selection from moral hazard in health insurance markets?
column2: Adverse selection: consumers possess private information about health status that insurers cannot observe (pre-existing asymmetry). Moral hazard: insured individuals change behavior/consumption after obtaining coverage because they no longer bear the full marginal cost.

column1: In the basic health insurance model, what is a consumer's expected utility WITHOUT insurance, given probability p of staying healthy (wealth W) and probability (1-p) of illness (wealth W-M)?
What is the actuarially fair premium condition for an insurance contract with indemnity I and illness probability (1-p)?
column2: π = (1-p)·I — the premium equals the expected cost to the insurer.

column1: Why does a risk-averse consumer prefer full actuarially-fair insurance to no insurance, in terms of the utility function's mathematical property?
column2: Because u(c) is concave (u''(c) < 0), Jensen's inequality guarantees that equalizing consumption across states (via insurance) yields higher expected utility than facing the uninsured lottery, even though expected wealth is unchanged.

column1: Under full insurance (I = M) with an actuarially fair premium, what does the consumer's expected utility reduce to?
column2: E[U_insurance] = u(W - (1-p)M) — consumption is fully equalized across states, so expected utility equals the utility of certain consumption at that level.

column1: What four conditions must hold for competitive markets to achieve Pareto efficiency, and how does healthcare violate them?
column2: Perfect information, no externalities, complete markets, and price-taking rational actors. Healthcare violates nearly all: information asymmetry, provider-induced demand, incomplete insurance markets, and agency problems distort price signals.

column1: What is a QALY and how is it calculated for a health intervention?
column2: A Quality-Adjusted Life Year represents one year of life in perfect health; years are weighted by a quality factor from 0 (death) to 1 (perfect health). E.g., 1 year lived at quality weight 0.7 generates 0.7 QALYs.

column1: What is the canonical health production function invariant in health policy evaluation, and what is its core identification challenge?
column2: H_i = f(X_i, ε_i), where H_i is health status, X_i is health-relevant inputs, and ε_i is unobserved heterogeneity/shocks. The core challenge is identifying causal parameters of f(·) when treatment assignment is non-random and individuals self-select based on unobserved severity.
